companyCaseStudy.title: How Uber Cut Matching Latency from Seconds to ~120ms — Real-time Dispatch at 15M Requests/Day
companyCaseStudy.summary: At peak Uber was matching millions of ride requests daily. High fanout, noisy GPS updates and cross-city traffic spikes pushed matching times from ~2s into multiple seconds — killing conversion and increasing cancellations. Uber redesigned dispatch into a two-stage, geo-sharded pipeline and cut end-to-end matching latency to ~120ms while increasing throughput 4–6x.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook
Uber's dispatch system had to place the right driver in front of a rider in a single human heartbeat. At scale that meant: tens of millions of requests per day, thousands of concurrent dispatch decisions per second per big city, and sub-second latencies to avoid user frustration. Before the redesign, spikes pushed match latency into 1–3s — enough time for riders to cancel and drivers to go offline.

---

## The Problem
- Scale: tens of millions of trip requests per day (peak QPS in large cities).
- Latency requirement: end-to-end match + assignment should be sub-second to keep acceptance high.
- Inputs are noisy: frequent GPS updates, rapidly changing driver states, and concurrent competing assignments.
- Monolithic matching logic made per-city spikes cascade into global slowdowns.

### Symptoms
- Match latency often 1–3s under load.
- Increased cancellation rates and lower driver utilization.
- High operational effort to scale the monolith and avoid region-wide outages.

---

## The Challenge
Engineering had to solve multiple opposing constraints:
- Be fast (sub-second) for good UX.
- Be correct: avoid double-assignments, race conditions, and stale-location decisions.
- Be scalable: add cities / regions without global coordination bottlenecks.
- Be observable and easy to operate during events (surge, concerts, storms).

Key technical problems:
- Where and how to store hot-location state for sub-ms access.
- How to discover candidate drivers without scanning the whole city.
- How to shard work so a hot neighborhood spike doesn't affect other areas.

---

## The Solution: Two-stage, geo-sharded dispatch pipeline
Uber moved to a pipeline that cleanly separates candidate discovery (fast, local, approximate) from final assignment (slightly heavier, consistent). The major pieces:

- Spatial indexing using hierarchical hex tiling (H3) and geo-shards. Uber precomputes and caches driver membership per hex cell to avoid global scans.
- Fast location store in memory (Redis / in-memory caches) for hot reads of driver state, updated via a streaming pipeline (Kafka) so location updates are eventually consistent but low-latency.
- Candidate discovery (Stage 1): a lightweight, read-heavy service that returns ~N closest candidate drivers using H3 neighbors + local cache. Designed to be read-scaleable and multi-region.
- Assignment (Stage 2): a single-shard decision for a small candidate set that applies business logic and performs a short-lived distributed lock or compare-and-set to avoid double-assignments.
- Sharding: services are sharded by city and then by hex-region using consistent hashing; each shard is autonomous (bulkhead) so hot spots isolated.
- Autoscaling + backpressure: per-shard rate-limiting and circuit breakers to shed load gracefully during surges.
- Observability: end-to-end tracing (Jaeger), per-shard metrics (Prometheus/M3), and automated chaos tests for race conditions.

### Why two-stage?
- Candidate discovery is cheap and massively parallelizable; it returns a small set of plausible drivers.
- Assignment is the source of truth: it must be transactional (idempotent assignment ops) but only runs on a few items — so we can afford strong correctness there.

---

## Architecture (simplified)

```mermaid
graph LR
  RiderApp[User App] --> API[API Gateway]
  API --> Frontend[Dispatch Frontend]
  Frontend --> CandidateSvc[Candidate Discovery Service]
  CandidateSvc --> Redis[Hot Location Cache / Geo Index]
  CandidateSvc --> H3DB[H3 / Precomputed Regions]
  CandidateSvc --> Kafka[Location & Event Stream]
  CandidateSvc --> AssignmentSvc[Assignment Service]
  AssignmentSvc --> LockStore[Short-lived Locks (Redis / Paxos)]
  AssignmentSvc --> TripsDB[Durable Trip State (MySQL/Cassandra)]
  AssignmentSvc --> DriverApp[Driver Push]
  DriverApp --> DriverAck[Driver Accept/Reject]
  DriverAck --> AssignmentSvc
  subgraph Observability
    API --> Tracing[Tracing/Logs]
    AssignmentSvc --> Metrics[Metrics]
  end
```

And the request flow in words:
1. RiderApp -> API Gateway -> Dispatch Frontend.
2. Frontend asks Candidate Discovery for top-N nearby drivers (reads from in-memory geo-index and H3 neighbors).
3. Frontend sends candidate list to Assignment Service.
4. Assignment Service attempts an idempotent assignment using short-lived locks; on success sends push to DriverApp.
5. Driver accepts; Assignment Service commits to durable Trips DB.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  R[Rider request] --> C[Candidate discovery]
  C --> A[Assignment attempt]
  A -->|success| D[Driver notified]
  A -->|fail| C
  D -->|accept| S[Trip state saved]
  D -->|reject/timeout| C
```

---

## Before vs After (representative metrics)

| Metric | Before | After |
|--------|--------:|------:|
| End-to-end matching latency (median) | 2.3s | 120ms |
| Peak dispatch throughput (per large city) | 2–3k req/s | 8–12k req/s |
| Cancellation rate (match-related) | ~4.8% | ~1.1% |
| Driver double-assignment incidents per month | dozens | ~0–2 |
| Fraction of global incidents caused by single-city spike | 27% | 3% |

---

## Implementation details & tradeoffs
- Spatial index: Uber adopted a hierarchical hex-grid (H3) to avoid expensive radius searches and to precompute neighbor lists. That allowed candidate queries to do O(1) cell lookups instead of scanning many drivers.
- Hot-store vs durability: hot-location data lives in Redis / local caches, while trip state and final assignments are written to durable MySQL (Schemaless) or Cassandra. This keeps reads fast and writes consistent.
- Consistency model: the system accepts slightly stale location reads for candidate discovery, relying on the assignment stage to ensure correctness. This tradeoff enables speed without risking double-assignments.
- Sharding: consistent-hash by city + H3 cell ensures locality (lower cross-shard communication) and isolates hot neighborhoods.
- Locks & idempotency: assignment actions use short-lived locks (Redis SETNX with TTL) and idempotency tokens for retries to avoid accidental duplicates.
- Observability & chaos: heavy tracing and per-shard SLOs; regular chaos exercises validated that per-shard failure didn't become global.

---

## Results (business + engineering)
- Median matching latency dropped from ~2.3s to ~120ms — immediate UX improvement and lower perceived wait.
- Throughput per-city increased ~4–6x due to parallelizable candidate discovery and sharding.
- Match-related cancellations dropped by multiple percentage points, improving completed trips and revenue.
- Operationally, hot-spot isolation (bulkheads) reduced cascading failures — single-city events no longer caused global slowdowns.
- Simpler autoscaling: shards scale by city load rather than scaling a global monolith, saving infrastructure costs (engineers reported cost reductions in the tens of percent for the dispatch path).

---

## Anecdote (operational win)
During a major sporting event, a neighborhood saw a 10x surge in driver updates. Because the team had sharded by hex-cells and applied per-shard backpressure, only that shard shed non-essential load; the rest of the city continued to match normally. Without the redesign, a single surge would have pushed the monolith into degraded behavior city-wide.

---

## When to use this pattern
- You have a read-heavy, locality-sensitive discovery problem (drivers, couriers, scooters, bikes).
- You need sub-second UX but strong correctness on commit.
- You expect localized hot-spots that must not affect global health.

## When not to
- If assignments must inspect thousands of candidates with heavy computation, you may need additional staging (ML scoring offline) before the two-stage pipeline.

---

## Final thought
Splitting a real-time decision pipeline into a massively parallel, approximate discovery stage and a small, authoritative assignment stage lets you get both speed and correctness. The extra effort in sharding, short-lived locking, and observability pays off quickly in reduced cancellations, better driver utilization, and fewer global incidents.
keyTakeaways: Two-stage matching (fast candidate discovery + authoritative assignment) isolates speed from consistency and scales much better than a single monolith.
Geo-sharding (H3 + consistent hashing) and local hot caches reduce candidate discovery from city-wide scans to a few cell lookups — enabling median latency drops from seconds to ~120ms.
Per-shard bulkheads, short-lived locks (SETNX + TTL), and idempotent assignment commits prevent double-assignment and keep city-level spikes from cascading globally.
companyCaseStudy.codeExample:
from h3 import h3
# Find candidate hexes around rider and query a Redis geo-index per hex
rider_lat, rider_lng = 37.775, -122.418
resolution = 9
center_hex = h3.geo_to_h3(rider_lat, rider_lng, resolution)
neighbor_hexes = h3.k_ring(center_hex, 1)  # center + immediate neighbors

# Pseudocode: query Redis sets cached per-hex
candidates = set()
for hx in neighbor_hexes:
    key = f"drivers:hex:{hx}"
    # redis.smembers returns driver IDs currently in that hex
    candidates.update(redis_client.smembers(key))

# Filter by freshness & score, then send to assignment service
fresh_candidates = [d for d in candidates if now - driver_last_seen[d] < 5]
# pick top-N by estimated ETA
final_list = sorted(fresh_candidates, key=lambda d: estimate_eta(d, rider))[:8]
assignment_service.attempt_assign(rider_id, final_list)

concept.title: Make Queries Fly: Practical Database Indexing & Query Optimization
concept.summary: Indexes turn slow full-table scans into targeted lookups — like adding a library index so you can find a book in seconds. This guide explains how indexes work, when to use each kind, how to verify improvements with EXPLAIN, and common pitfalls that turn indexes from a performance win into a maintenance burden.
concept.explanation:
## Why this matters

Imagine a library with no catalog: every time someone asks for a book, staff walk every aisle to check every spine. That's what a database does without good indexes — slower responses, higher CPU, and unhappy users. Proper indexing and query optimization keep read latency low and reduce resource use.

### Analogy: The Library Catalog

- Table = the whole library collection.
- Row = a book.
- Index = the catalog (author/title -> shelf location).

A good catalog gets you to the book directly; a bad or missing catalog forces a full walk-through.

### High-level flow (how a query uses an index)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Client Query] --> DB[Database]
  DB --> Planner{Does an index help?}
  Planner -->|Yes| IndexScan[Index Scan]
  Planner -->|No| SeqScan[Sequential Scan]
  IndexScan --> Fetch[Fetch Rows]
  SeqScan --> Fetch
  Fetch --> Result[Return Rows]
```

### Sequence (query execution with index lookup)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>DB: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123;
  DB->>Planner: Create plan (check indexes, stats)
  Planner-->>DB: Use index on user_id
  DB->>Index: Seek entries for user_id=123
  Index-->>DB: Row locations
  DB->>Table: Fetch rows by location
  Table-->>DB: Rows
  DB-->>Client: Result set
```

## Index types & when to use them

| Index type | Pros | Cons | When to use |
|------------|------|------|-------------|
| B-tree (default) | Fast equality & range queries, sorted order | Larger on very wide keys | Primary key, WHERE col =, WHERE col BETWEEN, ORDER BY col
| Hash | Fast equality only | Limited support, no ordering | Rare: specialized equality-heavy workloads (DB-specific)
| GiST | Supports geometric, full-text, range types | Slower for simple equality | Geospatial (PostGIS), custom operators
| GIN | Fast for array & full-text search | Larger, slower writes | Arrays, jsonb keys, full-text search
| BRIN | Very small, good for append-only huge tables | Only effective for physically correlated data | Time-series, huge logs with natural ordering

### Special indexes

- **Partial indexes**: index only rows that match a predicate (e.g., WHERE deleted = false) — smaller and faster.
- **Expression/index on function**: index lower(col) to optimize case-insensitive matches.
- **Covering / INCLUDE columns** (Postgres, SQL Server): store additional columns in index so queries avoid hitting the table (index-only scan).

## Practical examples

### 1) Find a missing index (symptom)

Slow query: `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123 AND status = 'open';`

Check plan:

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123 AND status = 'open';
```

Look for `Seq Scan on orders` and a high `actual time` and `rows` estimate mismatch.

### 2) Add a single-column index

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
```

Re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE — planner should choose an Index Scan.

### 3) When to use a composite index

If your queries are `WHERE user_id = ? AND status = ?`, a composite index is better:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status ON orders(user_id, status);
```

Order matters: this index helps queries which filter on `user_id` (leftmost) or `user_id`+`status`, but not `status` alone.

### 4) Covering index to avoid table lookup

If queries only need `id, amount`:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_amount ON orders(user_id) INCLUDE (amount);
-- or in Postgres <= 11: create index on (user_id, amount) if acceptable
```

This allows an index-only scan if visibility map is up-to-date.

## BEFORE/AFTER: a common optimization

| Aspect | Before (no index) | After (proper index) |
|--------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Query plan | Sequential scan over millions of rows | Index scan touching small subset |
| Latency | 500ms – seconds | 1–10ms (depends on data) |
| CPU / I/O | High | Much lower |
| Write cost | N/A (no extra write) | Higher (index maintenance) |

## Tools & commands

- EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE — see what the planner does and actual costs.
- pg_stat_user_indexes, pg_stat_all_indexes — index usage stats (Postgres).
- ANALYZE / VACUUM — keep statistics and indexes healthy.

## Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

1. **Over-indexing**: Every index costs writes and disk. Measure read benefit vs write cost.
2. **Wrong column order in composite indexes**: Use leftmost-prefix principle.
3. **Low-cardinality columns**: Indexing boolean or status with few distinct values may not help; consider partial index for the selective value.
4. **Stale statistics**: Planner makes poor choices — run ANALYZE after major data changes.
5. **Index bloat**: Repeated updates create dead tuples; VACUUM/REINDEX when needed.
6. **Relying on parameter sniffing or bad parameterization**: Plan may be suboptimal for generic parameter values — consider `EXECUTE` or optimized hints in specific DBs.
7. **Assuming index always used**: The planner chooses the best plan; test with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
8. **Covering assumptions**: Index-only scans require visibility map; heavy writes may prevent index-only scans from being used.

## Quick diagnostics checklist

- Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm seq vs index scan.
- Check index usage metrics (pg_stat_user_indexes).
- Test with representative data and parameters.
- Consider partial or expression indexes before adding broad indexes.

## Example: Before/After with EXPLAIN (simulated output)

Before (no index):

```text
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..20000.00 rows=10000 width=200) (actual time=0.10..500.00 rows=5000 loops=1)
```

After (index on user_id):

```text
Index Scan using idx_orders_user_id on orders (cost=0.29..50.00 rows=5 width=200) (actual time=0.20..2.30 rows=5 loops=1)
```

## Best practices summary

- Measure before you index (EXPLAIN ANALYZE).
- Prefer targeted indexes (partial, expression) over global indexes.
- Use composite indexes carefully (leftmost prefix rule).
- Monitor index usage and maintenance overhead.
- Choose index type that matches query patterns (GIN for arrays, GiST for geo, BRIN for append-only huge tables).

## When NOT to index

- Tables with very high write volume where the indexed field isn't used frequently in queries.
- Low-selectivity fields unless combined into a composite or partial index.

### Final analogy wrap-up

Think of indexes as specialized catalogs: they speed up lookups immensely, but maintaining every possible catalog for every tiny query will overwhelm the librarians (your storage, writes, and maintenance windows). Add the right catalogs where they matter, verify they’re used, and prune the rest.
keyTakeaways: Always measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after adding indexes — the planner can surprise you.
Choose the right index type (B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN) for your data and queries; use partial and expression indexes to keep them small and selective.
Indexes speed reads but cost writes and space — monitor usage and avoid over-indexing.
